However, above 20 EeV, the anisotropy's amplitude decreases to $[(1.5 \pm 0.5)] \times 10^{-3}$, with no noticeable energy dependence in this higher-range. The anisotropy's quadrupole component shows two distinct patterns, one observed at lower energies and another at higher energies. The distribution of cosmic rays' arrival directions twice exhibits energy dependence, as seen in our quadrupole analysis, and in patterns of anisotropy that are dependent on time and last for four hours, seen in both dipole and quadrupole components. These patterns resemble those seen in cosmic ray data collected at lower energies, but with energy thresholds shifted to around 4 EeV. No significant patterns of anisotropy that are dependent on sidereal time were discovered in our analysis, either at lower or higher energy levels. The anisotropy's dipole component at higher energies shows a nearly circular pattern, with an angle of approximately 60 degrees, in contrast to the anisotropy seen in proton data collected at the Large Hadron Collider. No significant dependence on right ascension was discovered in our analysis, either at lower or higher energy levels. These findings increase the likelihood that the anisotropy in cosmic rays' arrival directions is caused by a source that is moving at nearly half the speed of light, with an irregular shape and a long, narrow area of activity that spans nearly 300 degrees. The discovery of two distinct quadrupole components, one seen at lower and the other at higher energy levels, adds a new aspect to this source's complexity, with possible references to the great attractor cluster, specifically if the source is moving at nearly half the speed of the cluster and cosmic rays are experiencing a kind of interstellar perspective. The time-dependent patterns in cosmic rays' arrival directions could provide a source's velocity and other features, such as structure and movement, thus making their study a vital aspect of astrophysics and physics. The success of cancer immunotherapy depends on understanding the interactive processes
between tumor cells and the lymphatic system. To gain insights into this complex
phenomenon, researchers analyze digitized tissue sections with computer models,
although a limiting factor in this research is the lack of suitable data. To address
this issue, we present a comprehensive public database containing scanned tissue
sections, alongside manually annotated measurements of lymphocyte clustering within
these sections. The data set in question focuses on the coexistence of lymphocytes
and tumors, as well as lymphocyte clustering in normal tissues. It comprises
digitized sections derived from public sources and private donations, totaling 704
images obtained through multi-spectral scanning techniques, with each image measuring
728x1004 pixels and containing 47 Mbps of data. The associated annotations detail
the positions of indistinguishable lymphocytes and tumor cells, as well as the tissue
section's stromal area, with a total of 150,029 lymphocytes annotated across the
database. This data set has the potential to guide advancements in computational
immunology by enabling the development of precise machine learning models capable of
understanding the complex interactions between the lymphatic system, tumors, and other
components of tissue sections. Furthermore, this initiative includes a suite of
evaluation metrics and challenge problems tailored to evaluating the precision of
computational models in analyzing lymphocyte clustering and interaction with tumors and
stromal tissue. By introducing this data set and associated challenges, we aim to
spark research focused on improving computational immunology and understanding the
complex behaviors of the lymphatic system through computational modeling. The data
set and related challenges are available online at https://cancerimmunodata.challenge.

To mitigate burst errors in high-speed optical communication systems, a method is proposed that combines Equalization using Weighted Least Squares and Minimum Likelihood Sequence Estimation. Initially, a weighted decision feedback equalizer is designed to reduce the impact of rapid channel variations, and its performance is enhanced through a maximum likelihood sequence estimator. The proposed method's performance was evaluated using simulated data and compared to conventional DFE and MLSE techniques. The results showed that the combined algorithm has higher symbol error rates than individual methods, but can handle burst errors more effectively. Furthermore, the method outperforms MLSE alone at lower SNR values, and has a higher tolerance for sampling intervals in excess of the symbol duration, making it an attractive option for optical communication systems prone to burst errors. The paper also explores various WS-DFE parameter optimizations, and indicates that equalizer length and weighting coefficient can be adjusted to optimize performance, although they cannot surpass MLSE's maximum tolerance for burst errors. The method's ability to handle larger sampling intervals also enables the use of higher data rates with smaller oscillators. The proposed method's ability to manage burst errors makes it a suitable replacement for conventional DFE in high-speed optical communication systems. The technique's potential is further highlighted by the relatively small difference in energy per bit to noise power spectral density required to achieve a certain error rate, which is comparable to MLSE. The method's performance is demonstrated at data rates of 100 Gbit/s and 160 Gbit/s over 10 and 2 km fiber distances respectively, with the proposed algorithm showing equivalent performance to MLSE at higher SNR values. The technique has the added benefit of reducing the computational complexity by a factor of 10-100 in some scenarios, making it a more practical solution for real-world applications. Time-series forecasts often exhibit non-linear relationships, making them suited for models that learn patterns within data sequences. TCNs have demonstrated high accuracy in time-series forecasting while minimizing memory usage. However, TCNs' memory-based connections make them prone to expanded model sizes and increased inference latency. We propose an innovative auto-dilation optimizer for unsupervised optimal compression of TCN models. By leveraging a dynamic quantization method, it ensures consistent retention of high forecast accuracy across compressed models. Experimental results show that the auto-dilation optimizer successfully achieves optimal compression of TCN models for both small and large scales, yielding a 5-fold reduction in model size and inference latency. The optimized TCN model delivers comparable performance to state-of-the-art forecasting models like ProMP and BrainZ. Furthermore, the auto-dilation optimizer's capability to provide a range of accurately forecasting models enables trade-off options for reduced storage and computation. This study utilizes data from the ALICE, ATLAS and CMS experiments at the LHC to examine the connection between the quark-gluon plasma's macroscopic behavior and microscale flow pattern fluctuations in heavy-ion collisions. Initially, an increased flow signal in heavier ions is observed, and this increase is found to be linked to variations in flow pattern fluctuations as measured by the volatility and skewness of initial conditions. Furthermore, an association between the quark-gluon plasma's viscosity and flow pattern fluctuations is discovered, with more viscous effects evident in heavier ions. A separate analysis reveals that the quark-gluon plasma's radial flow is influenced by the density of partons, with a distinction made between the behaviors of up and down quarks. This research provides a deeper understanding of the relationships between the quark-gluon plasma's microscale and macroscopic properties, and highlights the significance of considering initial conditions and flow pattern fluctuations in radial flow studies. It also paves the way for further explorations into the interactions between partons and the properties of the quark-gluon plasma in heavy-ion collisions. Additionally, it is shown that the ratio of higher harmonic flow in heavy-ion collisions is influenced by the quark-gluon plasma, and this ratio can be used as a probe of the plasma's properties. Lastly, a framework is proposed for studying the quark-gluon plasma's density dependence, with implications for understanding the macroscopic behavior of the plasma in heavy-ion collisions. This research is founded on data from the LHC, and is predicted to influence future research in heavy-ion physics at the LHC, FAIR, NICA, and CBM. Ultimately, this study is aimed at delving into the intricate relationships between the quark-gluon plasma's microscale and macroscopic properties, with further analysis needed to thoroughly comprehend the underlying causes behind the observed phenomena. The algorithm addresses an existing limitation of the SHOIQ description logic when mapping formulas onto first-order logic. Developed within the description logic framework, ALBA determines first-order counterparts and extended counterparts for inductive definitions, linking the two and ensuring the correctness of the first-order counterpart. Essentially, ALBA implicitly determines a first-order correspondent for an (D)LE-inductive definition from a knowledge base, encompassing both the description logic axiom and the first-order definition. ALBA's core mechanism involves a novel approach to solving a system of equations constructed from the inductive definitions and their first-order counterparts. The algorithm is proven to yield accurate results, and a practical implementation is also demonstrated through a suitable optimization strategy. Moreover, an existing benchmark set is utilized to assess the effectiveness of ALBA, and a novel benchmark based on the description logic framework is introduced for ALBA's evaluation. The outcomes demonstrate that ALBA's computation time outperforms existing methods for calculating first-order counterparts, especially for complex formulas. Additionally, a distinctive feature of ALBA is highlighted, where it determines the first-order counterparts for an (D)LE-inductive definition by modifying the original definition, thereby expanding its applicability to various logic systems, including classical logic with equality and hybrid logic with intersection. Lastly, possible directions for further research and development are also outlined. TV-PARX effectively addresses complex issues by incorporating a flexible, nonlinear time-varying mean component and abrupt changes in parameters through the use of a Bayesian approach and a change point model. The TV-PARX model integrates a dynamic formula for time-varying parameters and incorporates external factors that influence these variations. Notably, the TV-PARX model emerges as a notable alternative to other point process models, including point process models that address non-stationarity, such as the Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive and Nonparametric models. We discuss the TV-PARX model's statistical properties and the estimation of parameters through a Bayesian approach within a change point model. Furthermore, we examine the TV-PARX model's performance in a simulation study and real-world applications. We introduce a novel framework known as Neural Descriptor Fields that uses a learning-based approach, enabling the acquisition of manipulation skills from limited visual demonstrations. By utilizing a descriptor network to extract object-related image features and establishing correspondence between demonstrated actions in the image space and 3D object space, our framework derives a density-based object representation. This representation, Neural Descriptor Fields, can predict, in 3D space, the locations of objects given new, unseen images. To automate the process of acquiring new object knowledge without restarting from scratch, we developed a gradient-based optimization method for updating Neural Descriptor Fields by integrating demonstration videos. By leveraging this framework in a self-supervised manner, we were able to achieve successful results in multiple 3D object manipulation tasks, despite being trained on just the code provided. Our approach outperforms the current state-of-the-art, a dataset-specific policy learning system, in complex scenes containing various objects. Moreover, by augmenting Neural Descriptor Fields with a goal-aware optimizer, we significantly improved its capability to acquire new object knowledge. Through various experiments, we validated the capabilities of our framework, including its ability to generalize across novel viewports, objects, and tasks. Moreover, our work highlights the advantages of learning object knowledge through visual demonstration over alternative approaches. The source code is available at https://github.com/lingco-pku/Neural-Descriptor-Fields.

The SiD Detector is one of the two validated detector designs for the future ILC, specifically tailored to meet precision demands in the study of Higgs boson and QCD phenomena. The SiD's calorimeter system consists of a highly granular and metal-ceramic precombiner design, featuring 48,652 individual calibration units with finely interposed iron and ceramic layers, allowing for detailed measurement of iron's contribution to hadronic energy response. Given the iron's complex field pattern, particularly around hadron showers, calculating the energy response in isolation is insufficient, instead, the iron's effect must be accounted for within a full simulation of the detector. Utilizing highly charged hadron showers, the SiD's calorimeter system demonstrates an achievable jet energy resolution of $\mathcal{O}(0.1)\sigma$ at $\sqrt{s}=10$ GeV, along with a achievable energy scale accuracy of $\mathcal{O}(10^{-4})\sigma$. Furthermore, incorporating intrinsic spread and instrumental effects into the line shape of energy spectra, the SiD's calorimeter system can achieve instrumental explanations for shifts in peak position and width at $\mathcal{O}(10^{-4})\sigma$ and $\mathcal{O}(10^{-3})\sigma$ respectively, surpassing sensitivity requirements for the Higgs boson study, and also meeting precise requirements for the study of QCD at $\sqrt{s}=10$ GeV, and could potentially be expanded to higher energy levels. This study highlights the importance of comprehensive understanding of instrumental effects, and the value of precise line shape measurements in searching for new physics beyond the Higgs boson and QCD. The proposed design for the SiD's calorimeter system has been validated through various analyses, and is set to make a significant contribution to the detector's overall performance in jet energy resolution across different energy levels, while also making significant instrumental advancements that could positively impact other physics areas. The metal-ceramic precombiner design, allowing for detailed measurement of iron's contribution to hadronic energy response, has introduced a innovative approach to calorimeter system design, and could serve as a benchmark for future reference. The comprehensive study of the SiD's calorimeter system demonstrates the capability of achieving precision required for the study of Higgs boson and QCD phenomena, and could also provide insights applicable to other detector designs for the ILC, in addition to potentially expanding the sensitivity of search for new physics beyond the Higgs boson and QCD. A newly identified red giant anaolog from the high-metallicity globular cluster Tononzintla 2 has been discovered with exceptional chemical properties. This finding, resulting from the APOLLOS spectroscopic study, reveals the cluster's rich elemental composition and high concentration of elements, exceeding typical levels found in Gibraltar and Omega Centauri. With seventeen analyzed elements, Tononzintla 2's metal content ranges from +0.31 to +0.59, showcasing a higher than expected abundance spread of 0.28 in comparison to similar scenarios within Gibraltar and Omega Centauri. A unique feature of Tononzintla 2 is its absence of anti-correlation between elements such as carbon and nitrogen, notable in certain high-metallicity globular clusters. Additionally, the absence of multiple populations with distinct chemical compositions supports the theory that Tononzintla 2 is a low-density open cluster rather than a heavy metal globular cluster. More information is needed to confirm the characteristics of this unusual object. With an estimated age of 10.5 billion years, Tononzintla 2 is among the oldest celestial bodies in the universe, providing valuable insight into the early development of the universe and offering a chance to study chemical patterns formed during the first billion years of the universe's existence. Due to its ancient nature, Tononzintla 2 offers a unique opportunity for comparison with other ancient objects such as Reticulum 2 and Tucana 3. More data is needed to determine the cluster's true distance from Earth and comprehensive chemical composition. Precise measurements of the vertical aerosol optical depth are crucial for estimating the direct radiative effect of aerosols, and this study demonstrates that wide-field photometry can contribute to these measurements. By utilizing multiple frames from a single camera exposure, we can derive optical depths for different altitudinal ranges. This approach allows for the determination of vertical aerosol optical depths without the need for highly accurate calibration of the absolute optical depth. We applied this method to multiple sites, both domestically and internationally, and found consistent patterns of seasonal variations in aerosol optical depths at certain locations. However, we also found that these results are sensitive to the presence of clouds, and a simple cloud screening method is necessary to achieve reliable results. Through this process, we obtained aerosol optical depths at approximately 10 degrees angular height for six domestic sites and five international sites, and the seasonal variability was compared to existing datasets. Furthermore, we compared our results to previous studies using similar methods and found generally consistent outcomes. We also explored the possibility of estimating the aerosol optical depth at higher altitudes, but this proved less reliable and required further development before practical application. With proper cloud screening and optical system calibration, this method has the potential to provide accurate aerosol optical depth measurements from existing all-sky photometry datasets, enabling the study of seasonal variability and the direct radiative effect of aerosols. However, before utilizing this method for this purpose, it needs to be refined to handle a wider range of cloud conditions and optical systems. Additionally, there are opportunities for improvement through the collection of additional field data and the integration of external datasets, such as satellite-derived aerosol information. Ultimately, this method could provide a more widespread and cost-effective means of monitoring aerosol optical depths on a global scale. Nevertheless, more work is needed to fully realize this potential through further development and refinement of this approach. With this study, we are initiating a public database containing the aerosol optical depths calculated from wide-field photometry measurements, and we invite collaborations and suggestions on how to enhance this database through shared knowledge and expertise. This study is part of the "Aerosol Optimal Extraction" project, and the associated data and software are available at https://aaxe.science. This initiative aims to establish a framework for a community-driven project and to provide a starting point for further developments in this field. This paper outlines the methodology and presents the initial findings from this project, and it also introduces the associated code, which is published as an open-source project titled "Aerosol Extraction Pipeline"

Our framework evaluates projected 2D images and estimates 3D object poses, whereas the iterative refinement process refines this information by considering possible errors in projections. Our method converges through an expectation-maximization algorithm and incorporates 3D-2D projection functionality. This study examines the effectiveness of various numerical approaches, including finite difference, finite element, and pseudo-spectral methods for solving time-dependent Schr\"{o}dinger equations in quantum mechanics. We test and compare the methods by simulating the alanine dipeptide dipptide, a small biomolecular system consisting of ten atoms. The accuracy and efficiency of each method is assessed using precise reference solutions obtained through the Krylov subspace method with exponential operators. The evaluation is conducted for different molecule-initial state combinations and we determine the performance of each method based on its computational time and error in predicting energy levels. The comparison reveals notable variations in efficiency and accuracy across the methods, especially when considering distinct molecule-initial state combinations, thus highlighting the importance of carefully selecting numerical methods for complex biomolecular systems. The findings can serve as a guiding framework for experts in numerical quantum mechanics who strive to optimize their algorithms or develop novel approaches for simulating biomolecular systems. The specific algorithms evaluated in this research, along with their quantum chemistry implementations and corresponding results, are freely accessible online. The code used for the simulations is freely available for download and can be utilized for the study of small biomolecular systems. The integration of binary black hole systems, surrounded by a distributed matter, remains a complex challenge in computational gravity simulations. This issue is compounded by the need to account for the effect of gravitational radiation on the motion of the binaries. In this study, we examine the effectiveness of employing a mixture of dark matter and gas particles in the context of smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH). This approach involves resolving collisions between SPH particles and determining the specific energies involved. We consider a range of initial conditions for binaries located at the center of a rotating dark matter halo, surrounded by a coating of gas. The rotations of the binaries influence the motion of nearby matter, causing a difference in angular momentum that affects the orbits over time. In addition, the motion of binaries through gas generates gravitational potential energy changes. Our computations indicate that, although the effect of radiation is significant in such systems, even in gas-free environments, it ultimately causes a cyclic slowdown of the binaries. However, when considering various initial configurations and radiation patterns, we found that the effect of radiation can either accelerate or slow down binaries in gas-free scenarios. In contrast, environments with gas always lead to a slowdown. Furthermore, our findings show that, although the influence of radiation may appear minor in the short term, it has a more substantial effect in the longer term. It is also noteworthy that, despite the complexity of these systems, using simple approximations such as the swing-up criterion can provide a reasonable, if not entirely accurate, understanding of the behavior of binary black holes surrounded by matter. In this context, we also present a more comprehensive version of this rule and suggest it could be employed across a broader spectrum of binary systems. In conclusion, our study has provided significant insights into the behavior of binary black holes surrounded by matter, reflecting the importance of considering the interplay between gravitationally interacting matter, radiation, and collision-specific energies in such systems. In light of these findings, we propose that future simulations of such binary systems incorporate collision effects and determine specific energies in a more explicit manner. Additionally, we suggest that, to enhance computational efficiency, a distinction should be drawn between illustrative and predictive simulations. In the former case, a greater emphasis should be placed on developing sophisticated models, whereas in the latter case, greater priority should be given to developing robust, high-performance computational frameworks. In this context, we have already taken initial steps in this direction by introducing an open-source code for solving these complex problems. This study prepares a specific type of epoxy-based material, Stycast 1090SI, 
for use in sonic anemometer sheaths. It compares the acoustic properties of this 
material to poly methyl methacrylate (PMMA), a commonly used alternative. 
The experiments determined the acoustic impedance and attenuation coefficients 
for both materials at different frequencies and temperatures. Findings showed 
that Stycast 1090SI and PMMA have similar acoustic impedance values, but the 
epoxy has a slightly higher attenuation coefficient than PMMA. However, both 
materials have low enough attenuation coefficients that they should not significantly 
affect sonic anemometer measurements under normal conditions. It also became 
clear that PMMA's attenuation coefficient is directly proportional to frequency, 
while the epoxy follows a different proportional relationship. To ensure accurate 
measurements, sonic anemometers should be calibrated with the sheath material 
it is actually being used with, rather than relying on theoretical comparisons. 
This research is relevant to atmospheric science studies that utilize sonic anemometer 
data and can inform best practices for maintaining and operating these instruments. 
It is also a useful example of conducting technical investigations that involve 
designing experiments and analyzing data in an engineering physics classroom. 
These investigations can help students better understand the importance of 
experimental design and analysis in understanding complex phenomena.

We present a novel computational method for detecting polymers within images, based on visual features that can be flexible in terms of monomer composition. This approach represents a polymer as a connection of specific image regions, characterized by local texture and shape characteristics, that can also account for local spatial relationships. A newly developed metric measures the similarity between features associated with individual monomers, allowing our algorithm to efficiently identify the most probable configurations of a polymer given limited reference images. This algorithm exhibits improved performance compared to existing methods and can be applied to the detection of multiple types of polymers across various images. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method by accurately identifying proteins, peptides, and nucleic acids in microscopic images, utilizing both 2D and 3D scenarios. The detection of these biomolecules is critical for understanding cellular dynamics and function, as part of systemic studies of living organisms. The algorithm we present has a distinctive characteristic where the representation of a polymer is no longer confined to a single contour or surface, rather it is seen as a network of connected entities that can be further analyzed to better understand its properties and behavior. This paper introduces a novel attention-unstructured model called Dilated Dense Attention Unet, which achieves high accuracy in esophageal tumor segmentation. By leveraging dense attention within unstructured attention modules, the network is able to eliminate inaccurate distance calculations and effectively process raw MRI images. Unlike traditional models, this method does not require generated images from previous layers to be upsampled, thereby eliminating unnecessary steps and directly producing dense attention maps. As a result, the network is able to extract more precise and detailed information from each image, contributing to better overall performance. To further enhance efficiency, we reduced the output channel count of each layer by half, leading to a significant decrease in memory consumption and processing time. When tested on the ESOP-HOP dataset using the Dice similarity coefficient metric, the network achieved a 97.58% score, outperforming state-of-the-art baseline models. To demonstrate robustness, the network was trained on a dataset with only two training samples per image, achieving a 95.58% score. This indicates that the model is effective not only in complex medical image segmentation scenarios but also in tumor-induced distortion cases, and has the ability to handle very small tumor samples. A key advantage of this model is its simplicity, using only global and local attention layers without relying on advanced techniques such as feature extraction or data augmentation, making it an ideal choice for medical image segmentation applications where large datasets are scarce. Real-time formation evaluation is crucial in oil and gas exploration and production operations.  However, fast data analysis and accurate results are highly demanded by ongoing production engineering tasks.  To achieve this, a proposed approach, LM-EnRML, leverages machine learning models that are pre-built during the slow phase of the application and uses an enhanced numerical method to speed up evaluations on actual data.  By utilizing a combination of linear algebra techniques and modified iterative methods, LM-EnRML significantly enhances performance, yielding a substantial increase of up to 5 times in efficiency compared to other methods.  Implemented with popular open-source tools, the LM-EnRML approach provides a versatile and adaptable solution for various machine learning frameworks, able to support a wide range of models despite being devised with linear models in mind.  Successful testing results, along with a substantial speed boost, validate the approach and its versatility.  To facilitate sharing and to address potential questions, the source code and test data are made freely available online.  Furthermore, the LM-EnRML approach is now integrated into the Schlumberger's ECLIPSE reservoir simulation software as a real-time formation evaluation tool.  In addition, the code is also embedded in the OpenFOAM CFD package under the fractional step diffusion equation application.  The LM-EnRML approach has significant implications for enhancing the speed of machine learning models in real-time applications. This study explores the potential benefits of using corpus-level information to enhance named entity recognition (NER) models. By leveraging a fully pre-trained language model and utilizing corpus-level information, our model achieves significant improvements in NER performance. Our findings demonstrate that incorporating corpus-level information leads to a 1.57% increase in F1 score for the standard CoNLL-2003 NER task. However, when the task involves identifying entities from a pre-defined list, our approach shows modest improvements. We also examine the implications of using corpus-level information for NER models, analyzing how this technique distributes annotations across entities and influences model performance in low-annotation scenarios. Our results indicate a interesting dynamic, where using corpus-level information helps NER models benefit from annotations, but may not necessarily benefit from entity-level regularization. We conclude that applying this technique relies on the specific task at hand. Additionally, we observe improved model robustness in low-annotation settings, which may be attributed to the spread of annotations across entities. We have conducted additional experiments to examine the potential causes of this behavior and propose future research directions. All code and data used in this study are available for public access.

Considering a tropical quartic curve $X_t$ in the rational plane, we analyze how the rationality of its bitangents evolves during a twisting process of the edges in a specific order. Initially, all bitants are rational and correspond to algebraic rational tangents. As the twisting progresses, some edges become irrational, causing the associated bitants to become irrational as well. Our findings indicate that the rationality of these bitants exhibits a pattern that counts the number of twists that occurred, allowing us to derive a rationality criterion. Furthermore, we demonstrate that every possible combination of rational and irrational edge types within the set of twisted edges can be achieved. Moreover, we establish that the same principles apply to tropical quartic curves in the tropical projective plane. By establishing a one-to-one correspondence between certain pairs of edges in a tropical quartic curve and the rational components of its bitants, we demonstrate the efficacy of these techniques in the evaluation of the number of rational components in the set of bitants of a tropical quartic curve. Our research expands upon prior works by supplying numerous examples of twisting paths and offering a more sophisticated understanding of the relationship between the geometry of tropical quartic curves and their bitants. Additionally, we present several examples of non-rational tropical quartic curves whose associated algebraic curves have rational components. Lastly, we discuss the connection between the twisting of tropical quartic curves and the rationality of their hyperelliptical covers. Moreover, we establish a lower limit for the number of components in the preimage of the rational components of bitants under such coverings. This research was conducted with the aim of exploring the relationship between the geometry of tropical quartic curves and their algebraic counterparts. Located in coastal regions, coastal radar systems face a significant challenge in tracking targets due to the limited view of the sea. A new estimation approach, known as Time-Frequency Entropy Estimation, has been developed to enhance the performance of these systems. This method transforms raw data into a meaningful form using time-frequency entropy and entropy calculation methods. The novel algorithm is tested in simulation and real-world environments. In the simulation, it demonstrated a 50% improvement in localization error reduction. In the real world, conducted off the coast of Finland, it successfully identified and tracked targets, outperforming the conventional RCS estimator. The results indicate that this method can effectively handle non-stationary targets and accurately detect the speed and direction of moving ships. Furthermore, the algorithm provides precise distance measurements from the coast to the target. In difficult-to-penetrate areas, such as rain or sea spray, the method reveals the presence of a target, even if the target's speed and direction cannot be determined. In these conditions, the algorithm's performance is comparable to ideal estimation. However, further refinement is needed to improve its robustness in challenging environments. The developed algorithm has been implemented on a RedHat Linux server using MATLAB and MatLab ToolBox. The code runs on a single processor and consists of approximately 2000 lines of code. The algorithm's memory consumption and multi-target capability also require optimization. The developed estimation approach has the potential to enhance the performance of coastal radar systems, especially in difficult-to-penetrate areas, and could be applicable to other radar applications. The code is available for research purposes upon request. The developed algorithm has been tested and validated with data from the FINRAD coastal radar system, which is part of the FENRIS project, and has shown promising results. The diverse languages and cultures within multilingual societies pose an interesting challenge for NLP researchers. To enhance cross-language understanding, we propose introducing NLP research that benefits multiple languages. As an initial step, we establish a set of evaluation tasks and datasets across five languages - Arabic, French, Portuguese, Russian, and Spanish. Our assessment covers standard NLP tasks such as sentiment analysis, inference, text classification, and translation. Moreover, we organize the 2nd Humaine Challenge on NLP in Multilingual Societies, with participants submitting over 20 baseline systems across the established tasks and languages. The evaluation results provide valuable insights into the performance of contemporary multilingual NLP models, alongside various cultural and linguistic variations. Ultimately, our goal is to foster advancement in NLP research for multilingual societies through regular re-evaluation and updating of the established benchmarks. The data, models, and challenge results are now publicly accessible at our website.

To accurately calculate the energy loss functions for Tantalum oxides, accounting for the charge loss within a few angströms, it is essential to consider both local field effects and spin-orbit coupling. Using the full potential linearized augmented plane wave method, these factors are incorporated into calculations via the Herring formula and Gaussian broadening technique. Local field effects are found to significant, exceeding 10% and influencing the energy loss spectra by 1-3 eV, while considering spin-orbit coupling has a more subtle impact, largely modifying the energy loss spectra by less than 1 eV. Nevertheless, taking into account both local field effects and spin-orbit coupling yields a more comprehensive understanding of the energy loss functions, particularly in determining the onset of excitons and plasmons within Tantalum oxides. These findings can guide experimental research, such as EELS and XPS, by facilitating the interpretation of data and distinguishing between different states in Tantalum oxides. Moreover, this study demonstrates the importance of considering both local field effects and spin-orbit coupling in energy loss calculations, with relevant implications for other complex systems. In addition, our results are compared to experimental EELS data, showcasing the importance of considering both local field effects and spin-orbit coupling for a comprehensive understanding of energy loss functions in Tantalum oxides. The phenomenon of partisan sorting, or the separation of like-minded individuals into distinct geographic areas, has significant implications for the online dissemination of false information. Specifically, in isolated areas with heightened ideological homogeneity, individuals may be more susceptible to spreading misinformation inspired by conservative viewpoints. This phenomenon, dubbed "The Big Sort," can exacerbate the online spread of false information among users in geographically isolated areas. This study explores the empirical consequences of "The Big Sort" on the online dissemination of false information by analyzing Twitter data and demographic information from 286 US counties. Our results indicate that in areas with increased ideological homogeneity, users are more likely to repeat false information inspired by conservative viewpoints, whereas no clear consensus was found regarding the effect of homogeneous liberal views on the repeat of false information. This research provides a theoretical framework that can be applied to a broader range of scenarios involving the interplay between geographic homogeneity and online behavior. Furthermore, future research is suggested to explore additional aspects of this phenomenon and consider factors such as online content consumption and user characteristics. This study's findings are relevant to ongoing efforts to mitigate the online spread of false information and could be used to guide targeted interventions in high-risk areas. This study's methodology is transparent and accessible through an online repository, along with a companion paper that outlines the methods in detail. A significant restriction of conventional machine learning approaches lies in their need for significant computational power and extensive, expensive annotation. This is particularly true for deep learning models, which combine computational resources with extensive training and subsequent tuning of thousands of parameters. In contrast, linear models, another option, require minimal computational power and annotation, yet often fail to match the performance of their deep learning counterparts. This paper investigates ways to enhance linear models by incorporating elements of neural networks, allowing them to compete with deep learning models despite requiring low computational power and annotation. We demonstrate that with the addition of a single nonlinear component, a linear model can surpass the performance of a neural network, and that the inclusion of multiple components can result in a model that outperforms both linear models and neural networks. Additionally, we find that these models can be interpreted through the application of recent interpretation techniques. As a result, they offer a compelling alternative to traditional machine learning models, combining high performance with computational and annotation efficiency. We provide examples of improved performance on a range of classification tasks involving mixed data types, and demonstrate the efficacy of these models in real-world scenarios. We also make available several examples and data sets that can be utilized for further research in this area. This innovation has the potential to give rise to a new category of machine learning models that can operate with minimal computational power and annotation, and may give rise to a broader exploration of linear-base-composite models in various contexts. We investigate the complex interconnections between speech generated during teaching by observing others by observing the variations that arise from different demonstration types, audio instructions, subtasks, and errors. Our analysis reveals the underlying structure of concepts expressed through speech and their relationships. We discovered a distinct hierarchical pattern where basic ideas merge into intermediate concepts and ultimately form advanced concepts. This concept hierarchy is visible across all demonstration types, task instructions, error levels, and both action-based and instructional speech. We found that action-based speech follows the same hierarchical pattern as observed speech during demonstrations, but with differences in concept distributions. Additionally, we identified distinct concepts that appear during error-filled demonstrations, as well as during demonstrations for simple and complex subtasks. We defined our finding as the permanence of concept hierarchies and temporary variation of concept distributions. Building upon this framework, we were able to improve speech recognition accuracy by up to 9.3% using a technique called multi-task training. Our study provides a foundation for further research on the relationships between speech, observations, and actions, as well as the connections between teachers and learners. By identifying concept hierarchies and varying concept distributions in speech, we are better equipped to tackle the challenging problem of teaching through observation. We have made our data and analysis publicly available to facilitate future research in this field. These notes describe how certain classical Euler-Arnold equations, specifically those for the Schr\"{o}dinger, Klein-Gordon, and Dirac operators, fit into a broader context of quantum field theory, focusing on an associated optimization issue. The discussions that follow will illustrate the relevance of these equations to fourth-order nonlinear stability and convergence problems, with specific examples drawn from the quantum Harmond theory, nonrelativistic Hartree type, Abelian Higgs, and Chiral models. The presented results provide nonlinear stability results for the Schr\"{o}dinger, Klein-Gordon, and Dirac equations, with various potentials, including the Hartree type, with positive energy bounds. The text also includes recent progress made in solving fourth-order stability problems. All-sky cosmic surveys suggest numerous small-mass objects are likely lurking in the Milky Way, yet only a few have been directly identified. These hidden bodies could be detected through their effects on the motion of test particles, which would follow a modified gravitational potential. By utilizing the viking data and a machine learning approach, we have developed a method to identify an unknown Earth-mass object affecting the motion of satellites at a 90% confidence level across the sky. This technique reveals that the viking data indicate the presence of such a body at approximately 30% of the celestial sphere, or 180 degrees, and pinpoint its possible location to a circular region of about 10 degrees in the southern hemisphere. This finding, which doesn't align with the orbit of the Large Magellanic Cloud, may be attributed to a compact star cluster or an unseen dark matter structure. The effect of this putative object on the stars' motions in the galaxy's bulge and the Magellanic Stream could potentially be tested with pulsar timing or high-resolution astrometry. A common challenge encountered by medical AI models is limited diversity in their training datasets. This study investigates how models' performance is affected by the diversity of their training sets when applied to unfamiliar MRI images. We used a large dataset containing over 300,000 MRI images and employed a mathematical measure of diversity called entropy to assess the diversity of each model's training set. Our findings show that as the diversity of the training set increases, the model's performance also improves and eventually reaches an optimal point before declining. Additionally, we discovered that models trained on diverse datasets perform better than those trained on non-diverse datasets, and this can be achieved by incorporating data that significantly differs from the training set. We explored several techniques to incorporate diverse data, including training models on diverse subsets of the training data and applying transformations to non-diverse data. Our research demonstrates the crucial role of diverse data in enhancing model performance and suggests possible strategies for incorporating diverse data in medical image analysis. However, further research is required to fully utilize diverse data, given the risks of incorporating data with significant differences, such as adverse classification. Our study provides initial insights into the complex relationship between diverse data and model performance and encourages the community to explore and establish proven guidelines for effectively utilizing diverse medical datasets. Our code and datasets are available online for further research.

ORPNVMM is compared to NOVA-relaxed NVMM and the results show that ORPNVMM outperforms it by at least 2 times for small writes. Furthermore, ORPNVMM exhibits comparable performance to NOVA-relaxed NVMM for large writes. We examined the Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_3$ system to understand the effects of Cm on the crystal and magnetic properties. Gd and Cm are both heavy fermion elements with distinct ground states, and combining them into the same compound allows for exploration of the interplay between their magnetic properties. Investigating Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_3$ compounds with x = 0.5, 0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1, and 0 for both crystalline and magnetic characteristics, and comparing them to pure GdSn$_3$ and CmSn$_3$, revealed notable effects of Cm on both aspects. To determine the effects of Cm on the electronic structure, we compared the results to theoretical calculations using the FM method. Finding that Cm enhances the magnetic moment despite being an expected non-magnetic behavior in CmSn$_3$, we explored this further by determining the crystal and magnetic structure for each compound. Additionally, we identified a characteristic ordering pattern in the magnetic moment as Cm composition increases, where the moment raises with a rate of $\frac{1}{3}$, eventually reaching the moment of the pure GdSn$_3$ compound. This research lays the groundwork for a deeper investigation into heavy fermion compounds combining multiple heavy fermion elements, offering an opportunity to study the effects of distinct ground states on the physical properties and to explore the principles governing these systems. This study is particularly useful in informing the design of experimental and theoretical research on superconductivity in these compounds. For the finite classical Coxeter group Bn, we establish refined exchange laws tailored to its generalized standard elements, which, along with previous findings, reveal a distinct relationship between the Coxeter length and descent set of Bn's elements exhibiting refined compatibility. Additionally, we demonstrate that the refined exchange laws are consistent across the symmetric group Sn. Building upon this, we derive implications regarding the structure of the Bruhat graph of Bn, which include proving that the edge connectivity of this graph is (n^2 - n)/2. Furthermore, we establish a connection between the refined left action and a class of ascending chains in the finite classical Coxeter groups, which provides a generalization of a well-known result for the symmetric group. This work is based on collaboration with David A. Benson, Philip J. Shuttleworth, and Nicholas J. Short. Earlier related findings have been discussed in papers by Benson, Shuttleworth, and Short.

We investigate the optical properties of T centre ensembles in diamond, specifically looking at how these ensemble properties change under a wide range of excitation conditions, including those similar to those proposed for quantum applications. Our characterization involves measuring T centre ensemble absorption, emission spectra, and the time it takes for photons to be emitted (photon decay time). The decay times are measured using two different techniques. Initially, we find that, to some extent, the T centre ensemble emission spectrum matches its absorption spectrum, indicating that the ensemble absorbs and re-emits light in a similar way. However, there are some exceptions, where the ensemble emits light at a different wavelength than it absorbs, possibly due to interactions between nearby T centres. We also find that the time it takes for photons to be emitted varies greatly, anywhere from a few microseconds to over 100 seconds, and is heavily influenced by the presence of certain nitrogen-vacancy pairs, which can both facilitate the exchange of energy between T centres and hinder photon emission. Some of our measurements reveal a significant, unexplained feature - a sudden and subtle shift in the ensemble's emission spectrum when changing from low to high excitation levels, despite both situations showing similar photon decay times. Different object detection methods suit varying practical purposes, and in many cases, real-world applications involve multiple object detection approaches. This paper addresses this issue by proposing a method to combine multiple object detectors. We develop an end-to-end formula to calculate the total detection confidence for overlapping detections, drawing from the predictions of multiple base models. To address difficulties with detecting, we introduce an adaptive threshold for practical use and leverage advanced sampling techniques for improved performance. The benefits of this approach are demonstrated through simultaneous use of one-dimensional and two-dimensional object detectors, resulting in enhanced average precision. Code is openly accessible for reference and further development.

This paper investigates a class of sublinear elliptic systems of differential equations of the PDE type. The equation has the form 
$\displaystyle \mathcal{L}_i(u_i) = \lambda_i u_i,$
where $\displaystyle \mathcal{L}_i$ represents a linear differential operator, $\displaystyle \lambda_i$ are eigenvalues, and the function $\displaystyle f_i$ satisfies sublinear growth conditions. By drawing on the Schauder fixed point theorem, we establish the existence of solutions to this system of equations under specific technical assumptions. Additionally, we examine the situation where $\displaystyle f_i$ exhibits superlinear growth, and discuss its implications for the existence of solutions. An important aspect of this work is the demonstration of compactness for the operator $\displaystyle C^1_0(\overline{\Omega})\hookrightarrow L^q(\Omega)$. This demonstration relies on a variety of techniques, including the compact embedding theorem, Poincaré's inequality, and a type of Poincaré's inequality for functions with zero boundary values. When $\displaystyle f_i$ is superlinear, we discuss the implications for the nonexistence of solutions to this system of equations. This work is inspired by the contributions of Lin in his paper 'Some regularity results for semilinear elliptic equations'.

This research introduces a novel approach to learning embeddings for natural language, driven by the need to improve the representation of language in datasets like financial news. The standard method of learning embeddings, via word2vec, falls short in this context because it mistakenly treats opposites like "buy" and "sell" as common synonyms. This is problematic because it affects the quality of the embeddings when dealt with individually, resulting in inaccurate predictions in machine learning tasks. To address this issue, we propose a novel loss function, named hitloss, that learns to place opposites at a distance from each other in the embedding space. To demonstrate the effectiveness of hitloss, we created two datasets containing the opposites "buy" and "sell" as well as "undervalued" and "overvalued". The experimental results show hitloss enhances the quality of the embeddings in comparison to the conventional method. Furthermore, our research finds hitloss to be particularly beneficial when dealing with limited amounts of data. Ultimately, our findings suggest hitloss offers a viable alternative to the conventional method of learning embeddings, especially in scenarios involving few examples. This approach is applicable to a wide range of tasks and datasets, including the two financial datasets used in this research. Ultimately, this research lays the groundwork for exploring other methods of learning embeddings that prioritize specific cooccurrence patterns. The code and data used in this research are available for download at https://github.com/ashish2610/hitloss.

A new stochastic method is introduced to overcome the limitations of the Fourier method in modeling Rayleigh--Bénard instability. In multiagent settings, agents can quickly discover actions that provide short-term benefits but ultimately lead to unfavorable outcomes through an action's elimination of better options. This phenomenon, where an action is successfully removed by another action, isn't commonly observed in discrete action spaces with numerous options. However, the frequency of such phenomena is heightened in continuous action spaces, making them challenging to learn from. To address this issue, we propose using an alternative loss function in value-based algorithms that encourages agents to shun actions that are consistently outperformed by others, even if those actions are rarely encountered. By incorporating a distinction metric that measures the difference between actions, we learn the weights explicitly to enhance the artificial potential field that steers agents away from undesirable actions. The resulting algorithm, a value-based retrospective optimization method, is designed to enhance artificial potential fields through the reinforcement learning process by minimizing the difference between actions that are and aren't part of the undesirable set. We evaluate our algorithm in continuous multiagent settings, using the benchmark games of multi-agent control and the studies of agent environments. The results show that it induces a potential field that prevents agents from learning dominated actions and facilitates the discovery of action trajectories that avoid iteratively dominated actions. Moreover, the natural policy learned through this process meets the criteria for being free of dominated actions in theoretical terms. Human subject experiments reveal that when agents follow this policy, human players can learn to avoid dominated actions within a relatively low number of episodes in the multi-agent control benchmark game. The success of our algorithm is a significant breakthrough in value-based algorithms for multiagent learning, allowing agents to discover the advantages of action avoidance through retrospective optimization. Inspired by contemporary epidemiological research, we develop a stochastic model
where individuals are represented as nodes in a random connection space. We examine how
the structure of the underlying network affects the spread of an epidemic. Specifically,
we investigate the impact of regularly disrupting and rebuilding connections among
infected and susceptible individuals on the final stage of the epidemic. Through various
methods, we analyze and compare the results of continuous connection modification with
discrete versions where all transactions occur at set times. Our findings demonstrate
that both the discrete and continuous versions share similar characteristics and can be
described by an exponential distribution. Furthermore, we discover that the probability
of infection follows a specific pattern that depends solely on the probability of a single
connection being infected. This enables us to establish a minimum condition for
infection and a corresponding threshold for the structure of the network. Additionally,
we explore how introducing distinct "groups" among the individuals affects the epidemic's
spread and find that it modifies the underlying structure in a way that affects the
final stage of the epidemic. However, this impact diminishes as the network becomes more
dynamic. Lastly, we compare our model's predictions with real-world data from actual
epidemics, obtaining plausible estimates for key parameters and observing that our model
can anticipate the epidemic's peak inflection point with reasonable accuracy. Yet, the
model falls short in accurately forecasting the eventual reduction in infection cases. 
This failure suggests that further complications, beyond the current model, are at
play in real-world epidemics. In the future, we intend to build upon this model, exploring
how additional factors influence the epidemic's course. The primary benefit of this
model lies in its use of a random connection space, providing a flexible and dynamic
alternative to static network structures. Consequently, this model may be applied to
a broad range of networks across various disciplines. 
Finally, the model's code is available for replication purposes.

A mathematical framework exists that describes how parton distribution functions (PDFs) change under transformations known as DGLAP evolution. This work demonstrates that using DGLAP evolution to fit PDFs by minimizing a sum of squared errors across various scales yields physically inconsistent results. Instead, we show that fitting DGLAP evolution to account for uncertainties at a single scale or multiple scales involves multidimensional Gaussian distributions, which can be represented using a single parameter - the radius of a circle that encapsulates a certain percentage of data points. This work also offers a new perspective on the evolution of PDFs within the DGLAP framework and reexamines the properties of evolved PDFs at higher scales, specifically addressing the issue of overfitting often associated with the determination of PDFs. Furthermore, we introduce a new parameter that directly quantifies the uncertainty associated with PDFs at a given scale, which can be used to modify existing codes such as xFITTER and ABINITIO. Additionally, we propose an alternative approach to fitting PDFs, which involves constraining the evolution of PDFs to account for the uncertainties associated with data at different scales. This can be achieved through a method called Lagrange multipler method, which allows for greater control over the evolution of PDFs. Our findings also indicate that the vast majority of protons' spin remains unaccounted for, which may imply the existence of new degrees of freedom that could be further explored in the context of small-x QCD. This work lays the groundwork for a comprehensive reanalysis of PDFs that incorporates uncertainties associated with the strong interaction as quantified by the vacuum energy density and pressure in the DGLAP evolution equation. This initiative has the potential to significantly enhance our understanding of the fundamental properties of QCD. This work has been finalized despite the crisis faced by theoretical QCD, however its core message remains valid and worth presenting. This work has been laid out in a way that is independent of the existing literature in order to facilitate a broader discussion of the topics addressed. In this context, the existing literature is perceived as a collection of personal experiences related to the evolution of PDFs. It is our hope that this work will serve as a foundation for a comprehensive reanalysis of PDFs that explores the complex relationships between the degrees of freedom associated with the strong interaction, the vacuum energy density and pressure, and the protons' spin. Using high-resolution laser scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy, 
we studied the superconducting gap in (Ca$_{0.45}$Ba$_{0.55}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$
films near their transition temperature. Our results show that the gap size,
approximately 0.1 eV, remains relatively constant around the zone corner, 
contrasting with the varying gap sizes observed in other iron-based superconductors.
Near the zone center and hole pockets, our findings support the lattice distortion 
scenario, while data from the electron pockets support the spin-fluctuation scenario. 
Our study reveals a diverse range of superconducting gap mechanisms across different 
iron-based superconductors and suggests that the gap size may be a critical parameter 
for understanding the interplay between superconductivity and magnetism in these materials. 
As a result, we propose that (Ca$_{0.45}$Ba$_{0.55}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$ is an ideal candidate 
for testing theoretical models of superconductivity through direct measurement of the 
gap size and its changes under external stress. 
By providing a systematic and detailed analysis of our results, we are also able to rule 
out previous interpretations of data, such as the presence of multiple gaps or the need 
for additional features in the spectrum. 
Ultimately, our research paves the way for further investigation into the fundamental 
mechanism of superconductivity in this material family. 
As the first experimental study of the superconducting gap in a metal without lattice 
disruption, our work sets a new standard for comparing theoretical models against direct 
experimental evidence. 
As a result of this study, we also propose that (Ca$_{0.45}$Ba$_{0.55}$)Fe$_2$As$_2$
is an ideal reference point for testing any new idea about the mechanism of superconductivity. 
Therefore, we anticipate that this study will stimulate further direct experimental 
examination of the superconducting gap in this reference material and other iron-based 
superconductors. 
In addition, we anticipate that this study will stimulate interest in exploring other 
superconducting materials that have not been thoroughly examined through LTS-STS. 
Ultimately, we hope that this study will contribute to the ongoing goal of understanding 
the mechanism of superconductivity in these materials.

We develop a novel Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation tailored to handle
spin-balanced hubbard models, and demonstrate that it yields the same result
as the superbosonization formula. To establish this connection, we employed
a two-dimensional lattice representation of the Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation
and applied the generalized Berezinskii transformation to map it onto the
superbosonization formula. Furthermore, we utilized this equivalence to derive
an exact diagonalization method for spin-balanced Hubbard models. Our study
also involves an intuitive description of the hubbard model using spinor field
theory, and includes a discussion on the applications and extensions of our
technique. We also successfully tested our method for both finite and infinite
lattice sizes. For instance, we used this method to compute the ground state
energy of finite lattices at half-filling, and achieved accurate results using
both exact and numerical diagonalization. With infinite lattices, we obtained the
exact expression for the half-filled ground state energy, and demonstrated that
this model exhibits a transition from normal to superfluid phases at critical
chemical potentials separated by the chemical potential of the hubbard model.
We hope that our study will contribute to the development of new ideas for
handling complex many-body interactions in lattice models.

We investigate how the thickness of LaNiO$_3$ layers within superlattices made from LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices of varying thickness affects the temperature dependence of certain relaxation characteristics. Our findings show that thicker LaNiO$_3$ layers are needed to observe the predicted phenomenon of increasing relaxation time with decreasing temperature. Ultimately, temperatures can be lowered to 20 K or less, depending on the LaNiO$_3$ layer thickness, before the expected temperature dependence is observed. This effect is related to the shift from carrier-mediated to hinge-like magnetic ordering within the LaNiO$_3$ layers as the thickness increases. Our research showcases the capability of LaNiNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices as versatile platforms for investigating the physics of LaNiO$_3$ films of varying thickness. Additionally, these studies highlight the potential for these materials to exhibit unusual transport properties, driven by their structural proximity effects, which could be applied to other heterostructures composed of different layer materials. Furthermore, this work predicts that certain LaNiO$_3$ materials with particular compositions may display non-ferritic magnetic ordering, which could potentially be stabilized within the 2D limit. This research also suggests the possibility of controlling the electronic properties of LaNiO$_3$ through precise manipulation of its thickness. Finally, we propose that these LaNiNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices offer an ideal platform for the study of spin-orbit coupling and other sophisticated phenomena unique to 5d electrons in 2D materials. Through the integration of theoretical and experimental approaches, our study provides a comprehensive understanding of the unique properties of LaNiO$_3$ when incorporated in superlattices and highlights the potential for further uncovering the complex physics of these materials in the 2D limit. This research may also contribute to the development of precise methods for monitoring the crystal quality and electrical properties of LaNiO$_3$ films, which will be crucial for the successful integration of these materials into various device technologies. Ultimately, we believe that this study will serve as a pivotal foundation for the extensive scientific research that will be necessary to fully uncover the unique properties and vast potential of LaNiO$_3$ in the 2D limit. This paper introduces the chordal Schramm–Loewner evolution (csle) on a specific time interval and demonstrates that it can be represented by a mapping that preserves order within the upper half-plane. By connecting csle paths, we obtain a surface known as the imaginary surface, which shares characteristics with conformally invariant processes such as the Schramm–Loewner evolution and the Brownian motion in the complex plane. By examining the surface's properties, we derive a formula that expresses the rate of growth of processes like csle and stochastic loop soup. Additionally, we establish a connection between the imaginary surface and the Löwner chain with a given set of analytic functions, which includes the Schramm–Loewner evolution and one-sided Brownian motion. This relationship enables us to classify the behavior of csle at both its starting and ending points. Finally, we illustrate the surface's properties through explicit calculations for processes such as the Schramm–Loewner evolution and one-sided Brownian motion. Developing large-scale distributed systems with accurate and up-to-date data relies heavily on Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs). Although individual CRDT designs are relatively straightforward, building comprehensive architectures using multiple CRDT components is incredibly challenging, if not impossible, to manage manually. Furthermore, ensuring the consistency of system maps that reflect the state of all replicas is a daunting task. To tackle this issue, we introduce a novel design approach, called High-Level Architectures for Distributed Systems with CRDTs, which incorporates map consistency constraints that can be broken down into pairwise constraints. We have successfully applied this framework to develop several prominent distributed systems, including Twitter's follower/following network and a distributed graph database. Moreover, our framework enables the creation of efficient replication strategies for each individual CRDT component, which can be combined to produce a fully functional distributed system. By utilizing this approach, we can guarantee that the system map conforms to the specified consistency requirements. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our design approach, we have developed a prototype tool that can generate replication strategies from high-level architecture descriptions. Additionally, we have conducted an in-depth analysis of several distributed systems built using our approach, which are currently in operation. The relationship between protein sequences and genetic phenotypes is not yet fully understood and is a key aspect that contributes to the complexity of the human genome. One way to gain insight into this relationship is by analyzing how protein sequences influence the effect of single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) on phenotypes. Here we utilize a comprehensive approach that incorporates protein sequence information to identify influence patterns on SNPs associated with various traits and organs in the human body. Here we refer to this influence as "protien mediating variation" (PMV). Here we determine the PMV factors for 175 different traits and organs and find that protein sequence influences the effect of SNPs in a bias-free manner, however it also introduces new sources of variation that are tied to specific amino acid positions within a protein. Furthermore, we find that the highest variation scores are associated with proteins located within cellular membranes and the effect of SNPs on these proteins is more difficult to predict using standard methods such as COE and S-scale. Our findings highlight the significance of considering the effects of protein sequences on genetic phenotypes and provide a foundation for future research aimed at better comprehending the relationship between protein sequences, SNPs and phenotypes. Our results and analysis are available at https://pmv.tocrf.org/.

This paper provides an overview of recent findings from the LHC involving proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV, specifically focusing on strangeness production. Unlike nuclear collisions which exhibit pronounced strangeness enhancement, proton-proton collisions reveal a less prominent increase in strange particle yields, characterized by little change in the ratio of strange to non-strange particles. Nevertheless, early indications of increasing strangeness with energy density, observed in nuclear collisions, can also be seen in proton-proton collisions. Moreover, data from LHCb suggest that the observed patterns of strangeness production may indicate the presence of initially produced strange quarks in proton-proton collisions. Furthermore, this could imply the creation of strange quark-gluon plasma like matter in proton-proton collisions, albeit with a shorter lifetime than that observed in nuclear collisions. Additional research is needed to fully comprehend the underlying mechanisms governing strangeness production in proton-proton and nuclear collisions. Nonetheless, the findings presented here already reveal notable similarities in strangeness production between proton-proton and nuclear collisions, suggesting that proton-proton collisions serve as a crucial reference point for understanding the physics underlying nuclear collisions. Additionally, this comparison facilitates a deeper understanding of the properties of the quark-gluon plasma produced in nuclear collisions. Lastly, it also enables a examination of the straggling quark behavior during the transition from proton-proton to nuclear collisions. 

This comparison deserves further attention from the theoretical QGP community as it may shed light on the microcausal factors influencing the creation and behavior of quarks within the QGP. Moreover, it may also provide insights into the relationship between the temperature of the medium and the quark distribution, as observed in proton-proton collisions, and ultimately, help develop more precise models of strangeness production within the QGP. 

In this context, we invite all theoretical physicists to contribute to this comparison by presenting their current views on the underlying mechanisms governing strangeness production within the QGP, taking into account the emerging patterns of strange quark creation in proton-proton collisions. This comparison has the potential to offer a new perspective on the physics of the QGP, encouraging a shift from studying quark properties in vacuum to exploring the effects of the medium on quarks within it. 

In this context, we propose the following questions to be addressed by theoretical models: 

1. What are the underlying mechanisms governing strangeness production in proton-proton and nuclear collisions? 

2. How do the results from proton-proton collisions modify our comprehension of strange quark creation in nuclear collisions?

The number of known neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries in the Galactic field remains limited, which makes the identification of the sole stable black hole X-ray binary candidate, V404 X-1, that of the longest recorded X-ray bursts, or the discovery of radio millisecond pulsars in this category exceptionally significant. By examining the Galactic field population of neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries and taking into account the discovery rates of radio pulsars, we determine that about 9 to 44 such binaries exist. If our observations are accurate, the ratio of neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries to black hole binaries could be as low as 1:10 or as high as 1:3. Furthermore, our study suggests that discovery rates of radio pulsars are influenced by the characteristics of the neutron stars, rather than the binaries themselves. In addition, we propose that the duration of the longest recorded X-ray bursts in V404 X-1 may be as low as 69 seconds. If this is the case, it could indicate that V404 X-1 possesses a type 1 X-ray burster with a normal pulsar-like spectrum. In this scenario, V404 X-1 would be the first stable black hole X-ray binary to exhibit this behavior, and its spectrum would need additional features to explain its X-ray burst characteristics. In this context, we also suggest that V404 X-1's X-ray burst spectrum includes a temperature of approximately 0.2 keV, along with additional components, and propose that V404 X-1's X-ray burst behavior may be similar to that of the neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries known as Zoland's variables. In this scenario, V404 X-1 would be the first member of this variable class that is not a discovery from a survey. In addition, we identify candidate X-ray binaries among the newly discovered radio pulsars, and outline observations that are necessary to confirm these X-ray binaries and clarify the relationship between the radio pulsar population and the neutron star low-mass X-ray binary population. Finally, we highlight that in order to fully understand the relationship between these two populations, more radio pulsars with high velocity need to be discovered, particularly those with masses greater than 1.8 solar masses. In this case, if the ratio of neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries to black hole binaries is less than 1:1, it would imply that there are a significant number of unstable or transient neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries.

While previous studies have estimated a key systematic error in this measurement to be around 0.05-0.1 kilometers per second, a new analysis indicates this error can be reduced to 0.01 kilometers per second when line velocities are taken into account. This more precise measurement of velocity dispersion is achieved by using line velocities to account for systemic errors in individual line measurements and by limiting the range of line velocities to eliminate extreme measurements. When applied to the Aricura star system, this analysis indicates a much narrower distribution of line velocities along its outer edge, suggesting that this system may no longer be considered a binary star system, but rather a moving object within the galaxy. Furthermore, using line velocities to measure velocity dispersion provides a more detailed picture of how the material within these systems is moving at different distances from the center. For the Aricura star system, this velocity dispersion is similar to that of the galaxy it resides in, indicating it may be a globular cluster, rather than a binary star system no larger than previously measured. This new analysis also raises the possibility that other wide binary star systems with circumstellar material may also be actual globular clusters. To distinguish between these two possible classifications, more detailed astronomical observations and modeling are needed to better understand the dynamics within these systems. Additionally, selecting candidate globular clusters based on their velocity dispersion and line velocities could provide a more effective strategy for identifying them. This new analysis highlights the value of using line velocities to measure velocity dispersion within wide binary star systems, as well as the importance of selecting suitable systems for this analysis, such as those with significant velocity dispersion and a range of line velocities.
